knowledge-base.overview: Go best practices from Effective Go and the Google Go Style Guide that complement lang-go.xml. Covers error wrapping strategy, context rules, goroutine lifecycle documentation, interface design depth, init() guidance, defer in loops, struct embedding, and testing patterns beyond the table-driven test already in lang-go.xml.

error-handling.description: Error handling depth beyond the %w guardrail in lang-go.xml. Covers when to use %w vs %v, sentinel errors, and structured error types.

rules.rule: Wrap errors with `%w` when callers need to programmatically inspect the error chain via errors.Is or errors.As. This preserves the full chain.
Wrap errors with `%v` when you are annotating for logging only, at system boundaries (RPC, IPC), or when you want to create a fresh independent error. This severs the chain intentionally.
Use sentinel errors (package-level `var Err... = errors.New(...)`) for simple, unparameterized error conditions that callers compare with errors.Is.
Use structured error types (structs implementing error) for errors where callers need to extract fields like file path, operation, or record ID via errors.As.
Never use string matching to detect error types. Strings can change; types and sentinel values cannot.
Do not add context that the underlying error already provides. Add only what the current function's scope makes relevant.
Avoid logging an error you also return. Let the caller decide. Logging and returning causes the same error to appear multiple times in logs.

context-rules.description: Rules for context.Context that extend the lang-go.xml guardrails on error wrapping.

rules.rule: Accept context.Context as the first parameter of every function that performs I/O, calls an external service, or has long-running work. This is the idiomatic Go convention.
Never store context.Context in a struct. Contexts are request-scoped; storing them creates lifetime confusion. Pass them explicitly through function parameters.
Never use context.Background() or context.TODO() inside a function that received a context as a parameter. Propagate the received context instead.

context.Background() is the correct root context in main(), in server setup code, and in test entry points. context.TODO() is a placeholder for "I know I need a context here but haven't plumbed it yet".

Cancellation interrupts the function — document context behavior only when your function does something unusual: returns a different error type on cancellation, or is NOT interrupted by cancellation for some intentional reason.

goroutine-lifecycle.description: Rules for goroutine creation and shutdown. The lang-go.xml pattern section covers WaitGroup and fan-out. These rules cover lifecycle documentation and leak prevention.

rules.rule: Never start a goroutine without a plan for how it stops. Document its expected lifetime in a comment: does it run until the context is cancelled? Until a channel closes? Until the program exits?
If a goroutine's lifetime is not self-evident, document it explicitly: "// This goroutine runs until ctx is cancelled or the error channel is closed."
Use context cancellation to signal goroutines to stop. Closing a channel is also valid but requires care (only close from the sender, never the receiver).

In tests, never call t.Fatal(), t.FailNow(), or os.Exit() from a goroutine that is not the test's own goroutine. These methods call runtime.Goexit() which only exits the goroutine it is called from. Use t.Error() + return instead.
Always wait for goroutines to finish before the test function returns. Goroutines still running after the test returns may reference the testing.T after it has been released, causing panics.

interface-design.description: Interface design guidance beyond the naming conventions in lang-go.xml. Covers when to define interfaces and where to put them.

rules.rule: Keep interfaces small — one or two methods. Small interfaces are easy to implement, easy to mock in tests, and compose naturally. The standard library's io.Reader and io.Writer are the model.

Define interfaces in the package that uses them, not the package that implements them. This is the opposite of most other languages. The consumer owns the interface; the producer owns the concrete type.
Accept interfaces, return concrete types. Functions should accept the narrowest interface their implementation requires. Functions should return concrete types so callers get full information.
Do not define interfaces "just in case" you might need different implementations. Define them when you have at least two implementations or when testing requires mocking.
Use interface composition to build larger interfaces from smaller ones: embed io.Reader and io.Writer in ReadWriter.

init-function.description: Guidance on init() — when it is acceptable and when to avoid it.

rules.rule: Avoid init() for most initialization logic. init() runs at import time, is hard to test, and cannot return an error. Prefer explicit initialization functions called from main().

Acceptable uses of init(): registering types with encoding/json or database/sql drivers (where the side effect is intentional), and verifying required environment that the program cannot function without.

Never put business logic, database connections, network calls, or file I/O in init(). These belong in an explicit setup function where errors can be handled and where tests can control initialization order.
Multiple init() functions per file are allowed but confusing. A single init() per package is the norm.

defer-patterns.description: How to use defer correctly, including the loop problem.

rules.rule: Use defer for resource cleanup: closing files, releasing locks, closing database connections. Defer guarantees cleanup even if the function panics or returns early.

Never use defer inside a loop for per-iteration cleanup. Deferred functions run when the enclosing function returns, not when the loop iteration ends. A loop with defer will accumulate all deferred calls and run them all at the end of the function, potentially holding resources open for the entire loop.
To defer inside a loop, extract the loop body into a helper function so defer runs at the end of each helper call, not the end of the outer loop.

Be aware that defer arguments are evaluated at the point of the defer statement, not when the deferred function runs. This matters for closures — a closure captures the variable, not its value at defer time.

struct-embedding.description: When struct embedding is appropriate and when it creates problems.

rules.rule: Use struct embedding for composition — to promote methods of an embedded type to the outer type — not for subclassing. Go has no inheritance.
Be careful with method promotion. All exported methods of the embedded type become methods of the outer type. This can expose methods you did not intend to make public.
Embed interfaces in structs to create implementations that partially satisfy the interface, or to build mock types in tests.
Do not embed a type just to avoid writing forwarding methods if those methods should not be part of the outer type's API.

options-pattern.description: Patterns for functions with many configuration parameters — option structs and functional options.

rules.rule: When a function has more than three or four configuration parameters, group them into an options struct passed as the final argument. This makes the call site self-documenting and allows adding options later without breaking callers.
When most callers use defaults and options are rare, use functional options (variadic ...Option functions). This avoids forcing callers to construct an empty struct.
Never use bool parameters to select behavior — they are unreadable at the call site. Use an options struct with named fields instead.

panic-recover.description: When panic and recover are appropriate. The lang-go.xml error handling guardrails cover the basic rule. These rules cover the precise acceptable use cases.

rules.rule: Never use panic for ordinary error handling. Panics unwind the stack and bypass normal error-return paths. Return an error instead.
Libraries must never let panics escape package boundaries except for programming errors (nil pointer, out-of-bounds) that are analogous to what the runtime itself panics for.
Use recover() only inside a deferred function. recover() outside a deferred function returns nil and does nothing.
If you recover() a panic that is not your own type (e.g. to catch parsing panics), re-panic anything you did not handle explicitly.
Prefer log.Fatal() over panic() for initialization failures in main() — it prints a readable message and exits cleanly.
Use "must" functions (MustCompile, MustParse) only in package-level var declarations and test setup where a failure is a programming error, not a runtime condition.

testing-practices.description: Testing patterns beyond table-driven tests (already in lang-go.xml). Covers t.Helper, subtests, error vs fatal, and test helper packages.

rules.rule: Call t.Helper() at the start of any test helper function that calls t.Error/t.Fatal. This attributes the failure line to the caller of the helper, not the inside of the helper, making error messages useful.
Use t.Run() for subtests to get independent, named test cases that appear separately in output and can be run individually with -run.

Use t.Error() when you want the test to continue running after a failure (e.g., to see all failures at once in a table-driven test). Use t.Fatal() only when continuing would panic or produce meaningless results.

Test helper packages that stub implementations should be named with a test suffix: `creditcardtest`. The stub types should be named by their behavior when multiple variants exist: `AlwaysCharges`, `AlwaysDeclines`.
Use the testify/assert or google/go-cmp packages for readable assertions rather than writing manual if/t.Error chains for complex comparisons.

quick-reference.item: %w when callers use errors.Is/As. %v at system boundaries or for log-only annotation.
var ErrNotFound = errors.New(...) for unparameterized conditions callers test with errors.Is.
First parameter, always. Never stored in a struct.
Only in main(), test entry points, server setup. Never inside a function that received a context.
Document how and when it stops. Use context cancellation or channel close to signal shutdown.
Never. Use t.Error() + return in goroutines spawned by tests. Wait with WaitGroup.
Small (1-2 methods). Defined by consumer, not producer. Accept interfaces, return concrete types.
Avoid for setup. OK for driver registration. Never I/O or business logic.
Never defer inside a loop body. Extract loop body to a helper function.
Composition not inheritance. Be aware all promoted methods become part of the outer type's API.
Never for errors. Recover only in deferred functions. Re-panic what you didn't handle. log.Fatal in main().
Call it in every test helper. Makes failures point to the caller, not the helper.
Use options struct (self-documenting) or functional options (zero cost for default callers).
